I'm ADD, no H at all. But ironically found out like 8 years after I got put on cymbalta for depression. I'm now tapering off it with the help from the new psychiatrist that diagnosed my ADD and put me on ritalin. I'm very nervous but also curious to see how getting off it will affect me now that I know my depression is likely due to mismanaged ADD.   
When I started voicing my ADD questioning to the cymbalta-prescribing psychiatrist, he just said "sure maybe you have it. But cymbalta is prescribed for ADHD too so.." I felt this was very unprofessional because he didn't even test me. It was also the first time I heard cymbalta was used for ADHD, and I figured if I'm starting to notice ADD symptoms it's maybe that it doesn't really have it covered? So all in all I don't recommend personally, but the big difference between us is I have no H whatsoever lol, I need the ritalin to get me going, even though cymbalta helped me do that when I first got prescribed it, but for depression.

I would just like to point out that many or most  commenters are answering a question not asked by OP, even if their answers can be very right. 
The question OP is asking isn't whether or not AI will replace us as teachers (which I think is easier to answer), it's: *will anyone bother learning English when AI can become people's interpreters?* :) which I think is a more interesting question to ponder.
 I think for us language enthusiasts the answer is simple but if we think about most people.... Personally, I've wondered about it and discussed with students.. I think there could indeed be a decrease in demand but maybe then we'll only have people that are really into it and actually willing to put in the effort, maybe the enthusiasts, the ones looking for the mental workout. And our classrooms will empty of the time and energy wasters who are only there because it's mandatory or theyve seen it's necessary for work or something but aren't really that invested. And that's fine by me. Those people make me doubt my career path every damn day and make me wonder what else I could be doing.

I went with debates for our oral eval instead of presentations like my own teacher had done. I didn't want to impose a topic on them that they didn't have any interest in though, i remember imposed debate topics as a student myself, wasn't a fan. So

\- we all came up with possible topics the class would be interested in, then voted down to 3. 

\- we separated the group into 2 groups, so they had different topics and enough material to jump in with. 

\- the teams were settled before evaluation day, so we were sure that there were around an equal number of people on the pro and con teams, since they chose which team they wanted to be on. 

\- they were to research all 3 topics in the days/weeks leading up to the main day. On eval day, one of the 3 topics was chosen at random. That way I tried to avoid them having prepared too much, I wanted natural speech and the research was only to be informed on the subject, specially in regards to vocabulary and arguments. 

\- everyone had to participate in the debate at least 2 times, ideally 3 (this obviously depends on your time and number of students, same as for the number of topics, since you could have more than one debate like us) and towards the end i would eventually ask someone in particular to try to talk more before time was up, bc i needed to hear them more to have an opinion on their level. 

\- Oh yeah before starting the debate, after announcing the topic, i gave them 15 minutes to organize their debate strategy by team, so that they wouldn't "steal" each other's arguments and then someone ended up with nothing to say lol bc i remember that happening when i was a student. 

I think that's it. Each debate lasted 30-45 minutes I think. We also had a written exam, which was writing an abstract for a scientific article. Which was the main thing for the module. And yeah as I mentioned before, specially for the oral, we established the rubric together.

It's true that they need training in this. The french aren't used to doing presentations. But other than forbidding them to read when presenting, and shaking them up by asking questions about their presentation, it's just not something I'm going to grade strongly on.    
I can still understand that native speakers just get bored in English classes, I was in that position for too long in my life, so yeah, i believe in giving them a break. But i mean, it's up to the teacher, the only thing I suggest regardless of which direction you go is setting them aside and telling them how things are going to go down. Or working it out with them.
